extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv coaches, and ensembles learning or performing the Harold longform
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and structural principles for creating and performing a Harold (longform improv) from opening through three beats and group games, including examples of openings, group games, and techniques for heightening and connecting scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3x3 Harold structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The Harold structure as described in Truth in Comedy: Opening; Scenes A1, B1, C1; Group Game; Scenes A2, B2, C2; Group Game; Scenes A3, B3, C3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Called the 3x3 format or 'training wheels Harold'—used to give improvisers a sense of organization. Del Close emphasized the format is for guidance and departures are allowed. Note: in the final set of scenes not all three will always return; players are encouraged to call back the most interesting scenes and characters and to intertwine them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening: explore the suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: After eliciting the audience's suggestion, the ensemble explores it for a few minutes in either an unplanned or predetermined structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbook opening structures include: a cocktail party that ebbs and flows between conversations; rotating monologues; invocation/occult-ritual style (It is, you are...); organic morphing sound and movement; pattern game (clover leaf word association repeated three times); source scene(s) used to pull ideas for later. Rarely is the opening just about the literal suggestion—the suggestion should be elevated from the commonplace to the extraordinary.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Beat (A1, B1, C1): three unrelated two-person scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the opening are three completely unrelated two-person scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each scene may draw on information from the opening such as details (location), themes/patterns (e.g., troubled family life), or tangential throwaway lines. The opening is a launching point for these scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group Game: palette cleanser and thematic binder
rubrics_metrics.description: After the third scene, multiple members return to stage for a group game based on the opening; it is a palette cleanser and should not relate to the established sets of scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group games can be 'scenic' (focus jumps among characters) or 'presentational' (focus on a concept). They are discovered as played rather than predetermined. Textbook examples: Advertising Meeting (entire cast creates an ad campaign). Presentational types: Flocking (mirroring), Simple game (rules developed during play, e.g., freeze tag), Slide Show (improvisers recreate slides), Inanimate Objects (short monologues from objects then scenes based on their relationships). Games bind the Harold together, explore themes, punctuate the piece, and provide variety so not everything is a two-person scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Beat (A2, B2, C2): heightening
rubrics_metrics.description: The second set of scenes heightens what was established in the first set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How scenes are heightened differs by school: ImprovOlympic often heightens characters and relationships (use 'Time Dash' to jump to a different point in time), while UCB may heighten the 'game' using analogous situations (e.g., bad cop -> bad priest). After the second beat comes another group game.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Beat (A3, B3, C3): connecting and merging
rubrics_metrics.description: The final set of scenes connects themes, characters, situations, and games from the whole piece; scenes often merge into each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all three scenes will always return—players should call back the most interesting scenes and characters and intertwine them. The third beat is usually the shortest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Everything in the world is connected
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial scenes should be very different with no obvious connections; in the final scene(s) the various threads should come together and connect (characters meet up or ideas/games/themes from different scenes converge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design openings and scenes with potential connective threads (characters, themes, ideas, games) so they can be woven together by the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvisers are pattern makers rather than storytellers
rubrics_metrics.description: Performers should follow emergent patterns rather than try to tell a linear story; they should not ask 'What happens next?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take what has happened and create other scenes, group games or transitions which create patterns with previous scenes and heighten that pattern as the piece moves forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-act correspondence: discovery, heightening, connecting
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadly, the three acts of the Harold correspond to discovery (opening/first beat), heightening (second beat), and connecting (third beat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this conceptual mapping to shape pacing, where the ensemble discovers ideas, intensifies them, then ties them together for an ending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harold eats everything
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything imaginable on stage—storytelling, dance, music, poetry, performance art—can be incorporated into the Harold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you think you can't do something in a Harold, you are doing Harold wrong. Be open to diverse forms and media in service of patterns/themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration guideline: 25–40 minutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Harolds are typically anywhere from 25 to 40 minutes long.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this range to plan beats, games, and pacing; individual Harolds may be shorter or longer depending on venue and ensemble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility and allowed departures
rubrics_metrics.description: Del Close emphasized the Harold as malleable—'the first rule is: there are no rules.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Departures from the 3x3 or other guidelines are allowed and considered important for a group's development. Content and the need to develop an organic commentary on the suggestion trump predetermined structures. Variations include staying as the first character versus playing multiple characters, whether the ending is a group scene, and changing scene partnerships across beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevate the suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening should elevate the audience suggestion from the commonplace to the extraordinary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the suggestion as a starting point to discover larger underlying themes rather than treating it literally; mine the opening for details, themes, and tangents that can seed later beats.
